title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.
status_note: The FSTTCS 2024 survey explicitly leaves this full decision problem open. The checked 1993 theorem is conditional on linear Schinzel/Dickson prime-tuples assumptions, and the 2017 conditional positive result uses the different unordered symmetric-prime structure. The 16 September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; source-open is a dated attribution, not certification of present openness.

importance.reason: A longstanding and foundational decidability boundary between tame additive arithmetic and number-theoretic predicates, with conditional definability of multiplication and direct links to prime-distribution conjectures.

sentences: Presburger arithmetic describes the standard integers using addition and order and has a decidable first-order theory.
This question adds a predicate for positive primes and asks for one algorithm deciding every sentence, with arbitrary quantifier alternation.
The resulting language can express prime-pattern claims such as twin primes and Goldbach’s conjecture.
A classical undecidability result is conditional on a prime-tuples conjecture, while a conditional decidability theorem concerns a different unordered structure.
An unconditional resolution would locate a major boundary between effective additive arithmetic and quantified number-theoretic reasoning.

definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.

source_formulation.text: Is Presburger arithmetic extended by the predicate for positive prime numbers decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question in its integer-and-order convention

context_blocks.text: Presburger arithmetic allows arbitrary first-order quantification but restricts its numerical operations to addition, order and fixed integer coefficients. Adding one decidable predicate can still change decidability of the full theory: the issue is the interaction with unbounded quantifiers, not the cost of evaluating that predicate at a known integer.

The source works over integers and writes an order-based twin-prime sentence. Accordingly, this card includes order and takes primes to be positive. For example, the twin-prime assertion is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\le y\land\mathrm{Pr}(y)\land\mathrm{Pr}(y+2))\).

The source also invokes Goldbach’s conjecture. Its even-input restriction must be explicit: one correct sentence is \(\forall n\,(n\ge2\Rightarrow\exists p\,\exists q\,(\mathrm{Pr}(p)\land\mathrm{Pr}(q)\land p+q=n+n))\). The printed illustrative sentence on p. 29 omits that restriction; the open decision question itself does not depend on this typo.

Bateman, Jockusch and Woods prove, assuming the linear case of Schinzel’s hypothesis, that multiplication is definable in the natural-number structure with addition and primes, yielding undecidability. The nonnegative integers are definable in the ordered integer structure, so this conditional obstruction applies to the present target too. The hypothesis is essential to the stated theorem.

Dickson’s prime-tuples conjecture is the assertion that finitely many integer affine forms with positive leading coefficients take simultaneous prime values infinitely often whenever no prime divides their product for every integer argument. The card does not assume this conjecture.

Kaplan and Shelah prove conditional decidability for the unordered additive integer structure whose predicate includes both primes and their negatives. Their introduction explicitly retains the number-theoretic assumption on the ordered undecidability result, although the abstract abbreviates that qualification. The absence of order and the symmetric prime convention are substantive differences.

The 2024 survey explicitly retains the present decision question. The September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; this is dated evidence and a search limit, not a proof that the question remains open.
